item.title: Tue AM · The Book Club | PragerU: Sir Niall Ferguson: War and Peace by Leo Tolstoy | The Book Club
item.itunes:title: Tue AM · The Book Club | PragerU: Sir Niall Ferguson: War and Peace by Leo Tolstoy | The Book Club
item.description:
How does war reshape not only nations—but the souls of those who live through it? In War and Peace, Leo Tolstoy sets Napoleon’s invasion of Russia as the backdrop for what many consider the greatest novel ever written. Michael Knowles is joined by renowned historian and author Niall Ferguson to explore how the chaos of war ripples through the lives of everyday citizens—from peasants and soldiers to aristocratic families. More than a historical epic, War and Peace is a powerful meditation on love, destiny, and the human spirit in times of upheaval.

item.title: Tue AM · Wildcard · Hit Parade: Going to Graceland Edition
item.itunes:title: Tue AM · Wildcard · Hit Parade: Going to Graceland Edition
item.description:
Four decades ago, Paul Simon broke out of a middle-age slump with a collaborative project few saw coming. Join Chris Molanphy as he explores the musical brilliance, polarizing legacy—and of course, the chart history—of 1986’s Graceland.

Captivated by a borrowed mixtape of South African music, Simon defied a UN cultural boycott and traveled to apartheid-era South Africa to collaborate and record with Ladysmith Black Mambazo and other musicians. The result was polarizing, critically beloved and, eventually, a chart smash. Graceland also set a new precedent for aging pop stars.

For an even deeper dive on the controversies behind the album, check out Ashley Kahn’s new book Days of Miracle and Wonder: Paul Simon and the Trials and Triumphs of Graceland . And for more on the anti-apartheid movement in pop, listen to Hit Parade’s episode on the rise and fall of the charity megasingle .

item.title: Tue AM · 60 Songs That Explain the '90s: Fountains of Wayne — “Stacy’s Mom”
item.itunes:title: Tue AM · 60 Songs That Explain the '90s: Fountains of Wayne — “Stacy’s Mom”
item.description:
A song played at every wedding, at every dance, and in every store, “Stacy’s Mom” has cast a great shadow over the rest of the discography of Fountains of Wayne. Today, Rob is here to shine some light on their prolific careers, commemorating the life of legends including the lead bassist and lyricist for the band, Adam Schlesinger. Fountains of Wayne are clearly a 2000s-sounding band, but their lyrics are reminiscent of bands from Rob’s youth like The Cars, giving them a timeless sound. Later, he is joined by music journalist Annie Zaleski, who shares her favorite songs from their catalog, how “Stacy’s Mom” became a novelty song, and the many different projects of Adam Schlesinger after Fountains of Wayne like ‘Crazy Ex-Girlfriend’ and the band Ivy.

Host: Rob Harvilla

Guest: Annie Zaleski

Producers: Julianna Ress, Chris Sutton, Justin Sayles, and Olivia Crerie

Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/60songsthatexplainthe90s

item.title: Mon PM · ShopNotes Podcast: ShopNotes Podcast E290: We Have To Have Turbulence
item.itunes:title: Mon PM · ShopNotes Podcast: ShopNotes Podcast E290: We Have To Have Turbulence
item.description:
What's the best inexpensive tool in your woodworking shop? And what's one tool you splurged on that was worth every penny?

In Episode 290 of the ShopNotes Podcast, Phil Huber, Logan Wittmer, and John Doyle tackle those questions and plenty more. From favorite woodworking tools and shop upgrades to organizing tool collections and protecting your investment, the conversation takes a few unexpected turns. And, of course, there's a little turbulence along the way.

The guys kick things off with listener comments, including more Shopsmith banter, oversized antique tool chests, and thoughts on Woodworking in America.

Then it's time to talk tools. John shares why he won't compromise on quality screws or a good router lift, Logan explains his appreciation for a vintage Starrett tape measure, and Phil talks about treating himself to a set of Japanese chisels.

Logan also shares how he's using AI to create an inventory of his woodworking tools, complete with estimated values. That leads to a bigger discussion about shop insurance, replacement costs, and an interesting question: If you had to rebuild your woodworking shop from scratch, what would you do differently?

In This Episode:

From ShopNotes Podcast, first released October 30, 2026.

item.itunes:title: Mon AM · The Diary Of A CEO with Steven Bartlett: Most Replayed Moment: Why You Need A Prenup And How To Avoid Divorce!

James Sexton is one of America's most high-profile divorce lawyers, with more than 25 years representing clients in New York, and the author of 'If You're in My Office, It's Already Too Late'. item.title: Mon AM · Wildcard · In Our Time: Archive: Citizen Kane
item.itunes:title: Mon AM · Wildcard · In Our Time: Archive: Citizen Kane
item.description:
Orson Welles was only 25 when his film Citizen Kane was released in 1941. It is widely acclaimed as one of the greatest, if not the greatest, films yet made. Melvyn Bragg and guests discuss Welles' film, in which he plays the lead role of Charles Foster Kane, a newspaper magnate. It was his first acting role. He also directed, produced and co-wrote this story of loneliness at the heart of a megalomaniac. The production was influenced by Welles’ experience in radio and theatre, and expressed the potential of cinema as an artistic medium with its use of deep focus, long takes and other techniques. The plot was partly inspired by the life of William Randolph Hearst, who then used the power of his own newspapers to try to suppress the film’s release. It was to take some years before Citizen Kane reached a fuller audience and, from that point, become so celebrated. With: Stella Bruzzi Professor of Film and Dean of Arts and Humanities at University College London Ian Christie Professor of Film and Media History at Birkbeck, University of London John David Rhodes Professor of Film Studies and Visual Culture at the University of Cambridge Producer: Simon Tillotson In O

From In Our Time, first released November 2, 2026.

item.title: Sun AM · Wildcard · In Our Time: Casablanca
item.itunes:title: Sun AM · Wildcard · In Our Time: Casablanca
item.description:
Recorded at the Crossed Wires Festival in Sheffield, Misha Glenny and guests discuss Casablanca, one of the greatest films from Hollywood’s Golden Era. The film stars Humphrey Bogart and Ingrid Bergman and features the unforgettable song As Time Goes By. Casablanca opened in November 1942 when Europe had been at war for three years and the USA for one. It was among Hollywood’s first major films to explain to US audiences why the war was worth fighting, and alongside this became a huge box office hit. It was created by a cast and crew full of emigres and refugees from lands under Nazi control. They produced a movie that has authenticity as well as astonishing emotional power that continues to this day. With Ian Christie Emeritus Professor of Film and Media History at Birkbeck University of London

Pamela Hutchinson Film historian and critic Sheldon Hall Emeritus Fellow at Sheffield Hallam University.

Producers: Simon Tillotson & Sam Peach Reading List: Rudy Behlmer, Inside Warner Bros. (1935-1951) (Weidenfeld & Nicolson, 1986) Thomas Doherty, Hollywood and Hitler, 1933-1939 (Columbia University Press, 2013) David Gerstner and Janet Staiger (eds.), Authors

From In Our Time, first released October 29, 2026.

item.title: Sun AM · Picture This: Photography Podcast: Why are all cameras Japanese?
item.itunes:title: Sun AM · Picture This: Photography Podcast: Why are all cameras Japanese?
item.description:
Tony digs into why all the most successful camera companies, including Sony, Canon, Nikon, Panasonic, Olympus, Pentax, and Fujifilm, are Japanese. SPONSOR: Go to http://squarespace.com/chelsea & save 10% off your first website or domain with code “chelsea”  The answer is complex, with 4 major turning points: 1) In the 1940s, WWII's divided occupation of Germany set it back, while the United States' occupation of Japan seems to have helped the Japanese camera companies 2) In the 1950s, the Korean war brought many photojournalists to the US-occupied Japan, and David Douglas Duncan, in particular, had great success with Japanese lenses on their Leica cameras. In the US, Joe Erinreich promoted Nikon heavily. 3) In the 1990s and 2000s, US digital camera companies (such as Kodak and Polaroid) failed to transition to the digital era. 4) In the 2010s, the transition from conventional cameras to smartphones saw non-Japanese camera companies (such as Samsung) exit the market. Japanese camera companies didn't have the freedom to easily exit the industry because of the legal challenges around layoffs. Sources * Software is second class: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GqMSWuSeDPA * This disc

item.title: Sun AM · The Mortise & Tenon Podcast: 71 – Finding Balance
item.itunes:title: Sun AM · The Mortise & Tenon Podcast: 71 – Finding Balance
item.description:
Do you believe it’s healthier to work with your mind or is it better to work with your hands? We hope you said, “Neither.” Why the dichotomy? In this episode, Joshua and Mike argue that getting stuck in one mode or the other to the exclusion of all else undermines a person’s overall health. We are more than brains, and we are more than bodies. Because of this basic reality, seeking to restore balance after a time of intense work is essential to be able to carry on to the next stage of life.

From The Mortise & Tenon Podcast, first released January 30, 2025.
